zones.label: Column 1
zones.note: Lexical cross-check: Entry Words Data of Nippojisho, NINJAL, Hideyuki Ohshima and Taichi Aida, version 202510, CC BY 4.0 (supplied page subset). The scan, not the index, determines the diplomatic text, typography, and physical lineation.

lines.note: Kiriyaburi means breaking through or destroying by cutting. This headword confirms the preceding page’s Qiriya- catchword; the abbreviated u and utta are retained as printed.
Tekijin wo kiriyaburu illustrates breaking through or destroying the enemy’s position. The Portuguese starts its explanation with the enemies and continues below.
Completes inimigos and alternatively specifies enemy armies. Fara wo begins the next example, concerning the belly rather than an army.
Completes hara wo kiriyaburu: cutting the belly open. The brief Portuguese gloss makes the bodily application explicit.

Kiro denotes returning, with cayeru michi as its Japanese explanation. Tornada is the Portuguese gloss. On second inspection the aligned provisional upright T and italic ornada are retained rather than normalizing the capital’s font to match the rest of the word.
Kiroo is an honored elder. The downward caron distinguishes this long-vowel headword from the preceding unmarked kiro for the return journey.
Kiroku is writing down or recording, explained by shirushi, shirusu. The scan supports eſcreuer, not OCR eſereuer; al- begins the indefinite object continued below.
Completes alguma cousa por escrito: recording something in writing. The tilde is retained rather than expanded to an n.

Kirokujo is a place in the Dairi or a lord’s residence where cases are heard and recorded, as the next rows explain. Dairi and Yacata are Japanese terms embedded in Portuguese. Retain the provisional upright initial Y and italic acata rather than silently regularizing the whole term’s typography.

runs.text: &c. onde ſe ouuem as partes dos que trazem

lines.note: Describes hearing the parties who bring legal disputes. The relative clause belongs to the place defined above and continues on the following row.
Completes the account of hearing lawsuits and keeping written records. No new entry begins with demandas.
Kiromekashi means moving or turning the eyes. The scan shows no comma between ſu and aita, so the abbreviated forms are not repunctuated to match other entries.
Completes the kiromekashi gloss: moving the eyes. This isolated noun is the object of the verbs on the preceding row.

runs.text: Qiromeqi, u, eita. i, Qiroqiroto ſuru.

lines.note: Kiromeki is equated with kirokiro to suru, the movement of the eyes. The second Japanese phrase has no internal break after Q; Mo- begins the Portuguese explanation.
Completes mover-se and specifies the eyes moving. The singular and plural Portuguese alternatives are preserved rather than harmonized.

runs.text: Adu. Modo de bulir com os olhos,

lines.note: Kirokiro is the manner of moving the eyes about. Adu. marks an adverb and belongs to the italic Portuguese apparatus.
Adds turning the eyes and illustrates it with me ga kirokiro to suru. The example is standalone Japanese following Vt, not an embedded term for whole-word font tagging.
Kirumono means clothing, literally something worn. The short Portuguese vestido supplies the entire gloss; the provisional st classification is preserved.
Kisan is explained as returning to the mountain, here rendered as returning to a Buddhist temple. The following tera example supports the specific institutional sense of the Portuguese varela.
Tera e kisan suru illustrates returning to the temple. The damaged middle letters are read with the headword and the preceding mountain-return explanation, not from a stale kana hint.
A separate kisan entry means coming back, paraphrased by kaeri mairu. The printed avir is retained, and Te- begins the enemy example below.
Teki ga kisan shita means the enemies returned. The scan shows a space before xita; the historical Portuguese ending in Tornarão is not modernized despite the past-time meaning.
Kisagi denotes a goldsmith’s scraper. The craft context confirms the scraping implement, not the similarly spelled return-to-temple entries.

Kisanji means relief or lightness of heart. The partly abraded initial belongs to Qiſanji, supported by the two derived entries below; the row is left-aligned as a headword, not indented continuation text.
Kisanjina describes something that relieves and cheers the heart. This adjectival derivative supports the damaged kisanji headword above; the object follows on the next row.
Completes the object of relief and joy as the heart. It is not an independent definition or entry.
Kisanjini is the adverbial form, describing a relieved or carefree manner. The abraded initial is Q; the Portuguese word has f in -fadamente, not the OCR’s long s.
Kisaki is glossed as queen. The long s in the Japanese headword is retained rather than read as an h-row f.
Kisaragi is equated with nigwachi, the second lunar month. The initial is Q and the usage label P. is upright; it marks the poetic register rather than belonging to the Japanese synonym.
Completes the gloss as a month of Japan. The historical accent in mès and Portuguese Iapão are retained; Iapão is not a Japanese embedded-term tag.

runs.text: Carta, falando com reſpeito da peſſoa que

lines.note: Kisatsu is an honorific term for a letter, expressed with respect toward its writer. The bare final t is the dictionary’s checked-coda spelling, not a missing syllable to add.
Completes the relative clause identifying the person who writes the letter. This ends the honorific-letter gloss.

Kisō is an honorific designation for a religious person. Enlargement shows a small circumflex on ô, not a caron; this corrects the first-pass reading while retaining the printed long s. The Portuguese explicitly marks the respectful usage.

runs.text: Ornato que ſe faz ſobre algũs manja-

lines.note: Kisoku names a decorative application on food or flowers. The explanation begins with certain dishes, dividing manjares at the physical line boundary.

runs.text: res, ou flores com folha de prata, ou ouro pe-

lines.note: Completes manjares and explains the use of silver or gold leaf. Pe- continues as pegada, describing its attachment to paper.
Completes the paper-backed metallic decoration and gives kisoku wo tsukuru, making this ornament. The Japanese example begins only after the paragraph mark.
Translates kisoku wo tsukuru as making this metallic ornament. Argentaria describes the silverwork-like decoration, not a separate Japanese noun.
A separate kisoku entry means a rule or law, explained by nori nori and Portuguese ley. It is a left-aligned headword, not a continuation of the preceding ornament entry.
Kisoi describes many people coming or gathering. Both printed long-o marks are circumflexes; the row begins a new left-aligned verb entry.
Kisoiki and the alternative kisoikitaru share the preceding gathering sense. The scan includes the final italic Idem omitted by OCR; the Latin l introduces the alternative form.

runs.text: ¶ Item, per met. Sobreuirem males, traba-

lines.note: The printed paragraph mark introduces a figurative extension: misfortunes or troubles coming upon someone. The final traba- continues as trabalhos below.
Completes trabalhos and illustrates troubles coming together with akuji ga kisoi kuru. The scan’s space between qiſoi and quru is retained.

runs.text: Ponta da eſpada, traçado, ou adaga,

lines.note: Kissaki is the point of a sword or other blade. The Portuguese names additional weapons; the scan supports adaga, not OCR adaça, and the headword is left-aligned.
Kissaki wo naraburu means aligning sword points. The mixed long- and short-s spelling in the example is retained rather than harmonized with the headword’s provisional double-long-s form.

runs.text: as pontas das eſpadas, &c. i, Darem muitos

lines.note: Completes the literal alignment of sword tips and begins its explanation as many men attacking together. The scan supports Darem rather than OCR Durem.
Completes the collective attack against enemies. This explains the preceding sword-point expression rather than introducing an independent combat term.
Kissoo is explained by yoki soo, favorable signs or tidings, and glossed as good news. Enlargement supports Qiſsǒ and Yoqi sǒ, replacing OCR Xiſsǒ and Toqi eǒ; both visible long-o marks are carons.
Kisugo is identified as a fish called mordaxim in the Portuguese gloss. The scan shows x, not OCR r; the historical fish name is retained without imposing a modern species identification.
Kita means the northern direction. The headword starts with Q, not the OCR’s G, and the gloss confirms the directional meaning.
Kitaku means returning home, explicitly paraphrased as ie ni kaeru. Portuguese tornada pera casa supplies the same homeward-return sense.
Kitaku suru is the example verb phrase, to return home. Italic Vt introduces it but is not itself Japanese.
Kitagochi denotes a northeasterly wind. The headword is continuous after Q; the gloss gives the direction without additional meteorological detail.
Kitai is something rare or unusual, paraphrased as yo ni mare na koto. The Japanese synonym belongs to the entry’s explanation, not to the embedded-term font-tag list.
Adds rarity and wonder to the preceding description. It completes the first kitai entry, distinct from the forging verb below.
Kitaina is the corresponding adjectival form, with Idem referring to the same unusual or remarkable sense. The apparent OCR gap after Q is not a word boundary.
Kitaini is the adverbial form of the preceding unusualness term. Adu. is the only printed gloss and is retained without an invented expansion.
The distinct verb kitai means hammering, tempering, or forge-working iron. The scan has a terminal hyphen after cal-, omitted by OCR, and both long-o marks are downward carons.
Completes caldear and specifies working iron in the fire. This anchors the entry in metalworking rather than the preceding adjective kitai.
Kitanabire concerns displaying or doing base actions. The description and its example are continued below; the initial belongs to one uninterrupted headword.
Completes the base conduct gloss and gives kitanabireta hito, a person characterized by such conduct. The Portuguese description of that person continues below.

runs.text: baixo de condição, & vil em ſuas obras.

lines.note: Describes a low or base character and vile actions. This is the evaluative sense of kitanabireta, rather than merely physical dirtiness.
Kitanai is glossed as dirty. The following two indented forms belong to this adjective’s inflectional or derivational presentation.
Kitanasa is the nominal form for dirtiness. It is printed as an indented derivative without a separate Portuguese gloss; none is invented.
Kitanoo is the contracted adverbial form associated with kitanai. The downward caron and the indented placement are retained.
Kita no kata here denotes the wife of a noble person. The separate following entry uses the same words in the directional sense.
The second kita no kata means the northern direction or side. The scan supports do Norte, correcting OCR da Norte.
Kita no hoshi is the northern star. The Portuguese gloss is retained as printed without adding a modern astronomical identification.
Kitari means coming. The short printed principal-part abbreviation u is preserved instead of expanding the full historical verb.
Kitsui is strong, harsh, or formidable in this gloss. The scan has v in terrivel rather than the OCR’s b, while its historical accentless spelling is retained.
Kitsusa is the nominal derivative describing the quality of being kitsui. It remains indented and untranslated in the canonical line, as printed.
Kitsuu is the associated contracted adverbial form. The visible u has a downward caron, and this short derivative is not treated as a missing body row.
Kitsune means fox. The long s in Portuguese Rapoſa is preserved independently of the Japanese spelling.

runs.text: Hũa maneira de grades que hà

lines.note: Kitsunedo denotes a kind of lattice or grille. The gloss begins its architectural location, continued on the next row; it is not a zoological extension supplied by the reviewer.

runs.text: em cima dos portaes, ou fronteſpicios.

lines.note: Places the lattice above portals or building fronts. The historical spelling fronteſpicios is retained rather than modernized.
Kitsuke here means comfort or something that revives and strengthens. This is the medicinal or restorative sense, not a modern clothing interpretation.
Adds vigor and gives kitsuke no kusuri, a restorative medicine. Mezi- begins the Portuguese translation across the line break.

runs.text: nha que conforta, ou dà vigor, & alento.

lines.note: Completes mezinha and describes restoring strength, vigor, or breath. The explanation closes the medicinal example.
Kitsukegusuri is glossed as medicine for the heart. The voiced g and long s are retained in the compound rather than using the separated phrase from the preceding example.
Kitsuki means coming and arriving somewhere. The arrival sense distinguishes this verb from the surrounding medicinal and color terms.

runs.text: Cor de caualo que tira hum pouco

lines.note: Kitsukige is a horse-coat color. The gloss describes a slight inclination toward another color, completed below, without requiring a modern standardized coat-name equivalent.
Specifies the color as tending toward chestnut or brown. This completes the horse-color description.
Kiten is quickness or sharpness of wit, explained by ki wo tenzuru. The Portuguese enge- continues as engenho on the next row.
Completes engenho and gives kiten no kiita hito, a person with ready wit. The source’s qijta spelling is retained; the Portuguese characterization continues below.
Completes the description of the quick-witted person as sharp and alert. It is the Portuguese conclusion of the kiten example.
Kitsuji is explained by yoi koto, a good or fortunate event. The final synonym is coto, not OCR coco; the bare t before j is retained as printed.
Kitsujoo is assigned the same auspicious meaning as the preceding entry. The long-o mark is a caron and Idem supplies the entire Portuguese gloss.

runs.text: Bom dia, ou de bõ agouro.

lines.note: Kitsunichi means a good or auspicious day, explained as yoki hi. The scan shows t before n in Qitnichi, not OCR u; bõ is a printed nasal abbreviation.
Kitoo denotes prayers or supplications, explained by inori and inoru. The Portuguese reads Deprecações, and a visible hyphen follows Qi- at the end of the example’s first row.
Completes kitoo wo suru, to offer prayers. The physical split Qi- / tǒ is preserved rather than recombined in the canonical transcription.

runs.text: Boa nouidade que ſe colhe dos campos,

lines.note: Kitoku here denotes a good yield or harvest. Portuguese novidade refers to the crop gathered from fields in this context, not simply new information.
Adds cultivated lowlands and begins the example: this year, compared with the usual. The final qi continues the adjective on the next row without a printed hyphen.

runs.text: Eſte anno foy milhor, & mais fer-

lines.note: Completes kitokuna and translates the year as better and more fertile than usual. The scan supports f in fer-, not the OCR’s long s; the physical break is retained.
Completes fertil and the comparison with the ordinary yield. This closes the harvest entry.

runs.text: Hum forro de pelles, ou de vimẽs

lines.note: Kittsuke is a lining or pad made of skins or woven withies. Its construction and relation to a saddle continue on f401; the separate tecidos beneath this row is only the catchword.
